title: Indian-American Teen Sharvi Mahajan Builds AI System to Detect Driver Fatigue, Named 3M Finalist
excerpt: The 14-year-old San Diego student's NeuroDrive Alert uses EEG and machine learning to identify microsleep before it causes accidents, earning her a shot at the $25,000 top prize.
body:
• Sharvi Mahajan, a 14-year-old Indian-American student from San Diego, has been named a finalist in the 2026 3M Young Scientist Challenge for her AI-powered driver fatigue detection system.
  • Her invention, NeuroDrive Alert, uses EEG sensors and machine learning to detect microsleep episodes before they cause accidents.
  • Five of the ten finalists in the 2026 competition are of Indian origin, underscoring Indian American dominance in youth STEM competitions.
  • Mahajan is competing for the $25,000 top prize, with the finals held later this year.

Sharvi Mahajan, a 14-year-old eighth-grader at Bernardo Heights Middle School in San Diego, California, has developed an AI system that can detect when a driver is about to fall asleep — and the innovation has landed her among the ten finalists of the 2026 3M Young Scientist Challenge.

Mahajan created NeuroDrive Alert, a system that combines electroencephalography (EEG) with machine learning to monitor changes in brain activity over time. The technology identifies early signs of fatigue and alerts drivers before they experience microsleep — brief involuntary episodes of sleep lasting only a few seconds that can prove fatal behind the wheel.

How NeuroDrive Alert Works

EEG technology records the brain's electrical signals through sensors placed on the scalp. Mahajan's machine learning model analyzes those signals to recognize patterns associated with drowsiness, providing a warning window before a driver loses consciousness.

Unlike camera-based fatigue detection systems that rely on tracking eye movements or head position, NeuroDrive Alert measures brain activity directly — a potentially more reliable indicator of impending microsleep. According to Mahajan, the technology could also be adapted for other high-alertness situations, such as operating heavy machinery or working overnight shifts.

Indian Americans Dominate the Finals

Mahajan is one of five Indian-American students among the ten finalists in this year's 3M Young Scientist Challenge, a premier STEM competition for middle schoolers in the United States. The other Indian-origin finalists are Aaisha Asif from Florida, Raji Doshi from Connecticut, Arika Kundu from Minnesota, and Naboshree Santra from Florida.

The pattern mirrors the dominance of Indian-American students in other academic competitions, including the Scripps National Spelling Bee and Science Olympiad events. It reflects a cultural investment in STEM education and competitive preparation that has become a defining feature of Indian-American communities nationwide.

The Road Safety Problem She Is Targeting

Drowsy driving is a major public safety concern. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimates that fatigue-related crashes cause approximately 795 deaths annually in the United States, though the actual figure is widely believed to be higher since drowsiness is difficult to detect in crash investigations. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that one in 25 adult drivers reports having fallen asleep while driving in the past 30 days.

Mahajan's system addresses a gap in current vehicle safety technology. While some automakers have introduced camera-based driver monitoring systems, direct brain-wave analysis offers a layer of detection that existing approaches cannot match.

What Is Next

The 3M Young Scientist Challenge finals will be held later this year, with the top prize carrying a $25,000 award and the title of "America's Top Young Scientist." Finalists are paired with 3M scientists as mentors to refine their projects before the final event.

Mahajan has said she envisions a career that combines neuroscience and artificial intelligence — fields where her early work already demonstrates both technical depth and real-world applicability.
